comment: The latency bars the project claims, and the benches that measure them.
Every read the server serves answers in under a millisecond, a page of an
expansion included (the owner's bar, 2026-09-05, tightened from the ten
milliseconds #129 set for a page); scripts/checks/bench-bars.sh runs the
benches and fails when a median crosses its bar.
Figures are microseconds: every bar is now met with room to spare, and
milliseconds no longer say anything useful about them.
A bar is the CLAIM, not a machine's measurement: it never moves to match
a slower run. `measured_us` records what one machine answered, so the
headroom a run has is visible, and it is a record, never a gate.
Each bar is a round number over the slowest median the bench has shown on
either machine that runs this check, with three to six times the headroom
(#304, 2026-09-23). Two machines run it: this laptop, and the shared
ubuntu-latest runner of the bench-bars CI job, whose medians over three
runs of the same code differ by up to 1.5x between runner instances and
are the slower of the two for the served operations. A bar set close to
its measurement gates on that spread instead of on a regression, and a
bar left at the millisecond gates on nothing: a $lookup that got twenty
times slower would still pass. Tightening a bar states a stronger claim
and is always allowed; raising one is not.
No FHIR or SNOMED CT specification governs a benchmark. The bars, their
shape, and the headroom rule above are this project's own design.
machine: Apple M2, macOS 26.5, release profile, 20000 synthetic concepts

bars.claim: a point read costs its answer, never a scan of the edition
validating a code is a point read, never an expansion
subsumption answers from the closure bitmaps, never by walking the hierarchy
a translation over a map reference set costs its answer, never the reference set
a page of an expansion is cut from the bitmaps before a concept is read
the served point read adds routing and the codec to the read, and no more
the served validation adds routing and the codec to the read, and no more
the served subsumption adds routing and the codec to the closure read
the served page of an expansion costs the page, never the selection behind it
the served translation costs its answer whatever the reference set holds
the first page of an expansion costs the page, never the selection
the layers every request passes cost microseconds, whatever the operation behind them
the SMART gate costs a version router and an absent issuer, never a token check no deployment asked for

served_comment: The bar a served read holds across every code system, checked against the
committed record set rather than the synthetic edition, because it is about
what a real system answers with.
A read costs a fixed amount plus the serialising of its answer, at a rate
that is the same on every system. A flat bar across systems is therefore
not a bar on the server's speed: it asks a 63 KB answer to serialise four
times faster than a 1.5 KB one, which is a bar on how much a system has to
say about a concept. So the bar has the shape the measurement has, and a
regression in either term fails it: a slower operation moves the fixed
part, a slower codec moves the rate (the decision on #512).
Confirmed against bench/records/2026-09-23-apple-m2 on 2026-09-23, the
first committed set that carries an answer size (#512). Fitted over its
seven systems, $lookup costs a fixed 97.6 us plus 4.61 ns per byte, and
all seven hold the bar. RxNorm's 387.7 us for 63,134 bytes is the largest
answer rather than the slowest read: SNOMED CT International pays 216.8 us
for 25,764 bytes at the same rate. The two rejected shapes stand. A fixed
narrow answer would stop measuring what a client is served, and returning
fewer properties unasked, which the specification permits, would change
the answer so that a measurement passes.
What the fixed term is made of, measured on 2026-09-23 (#628). Fitted over
the three `served/*_lookup` benches, which span 862 bytes to 63,134 bytes
in one process with no socket, a $lookup costs 11.9 us plus 3.74 ns per
byte. The same fit over a record set, which measures an HTTP round trip on
a loopback socket, reads 97.6 us plus 4.61 ns per byte. So about 86 us of
the fixed term is the socket, the client, and the kernel, and about 12 us
is the server. Of that 12 us, `fixed/axum_floor` puts routing at 0.7 us and
`fixed/served_floor` puts the request log, the metrics sample, and the
request identifier at 1.2 us on top of it; the SMART gate with no issuer
configured adds 0.7 us more (`fixed/gated_floor`).
The 28 us this file recorded between the 2026-09-08 fit and the 0.1.4 set
is the day, not the code. The server built from the 2026-09-08 tree and
the server built from today's tree were run by the same harness over the
same artifact, alternating, six passes each: the 862-byte ICD-10-NL answer
reads a median 104.7 us on the old binary and 83.1 us on the new one, and a
fastest pass of 78.4 us against 60.2 us. No change in the server moves a
term the loopback round trip sets, and the tree the earlier 70 us was
measured on does not reproduce it here.
The bar stays where it is. It leaves the smallest answers about 4% of
headroom on this machine, which is headroom over a socket rather than over
the server, so the two `fixed/` bars above are the ones that gate the cost
the server controls.

served_bars.measured: on 2026-09-23, over bench/records/2026-09-23-apple-m2: 862 B answered in 96.3 us, 7,368 B in 135.8 us, 26,725 B in 221.8 us, 63,134 B in 387.7 us, a fixed 97.6 us plus 4.61 ns per byte; in one process with no socket the same three systems fit 11.9 us plus 3.74 ns per byte (#628)
served_bars.claim: a served read costs a fixed amount plus the serialising of its answer, at one rate on every code system
